title: The Fire Beneath the Kettle
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 30 of 40
content:
The fire beneath the kettle was small, but Iroh watched it like a general. The riverside camp carried the smell of embers, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to ask him to share firebending that was not connected to war. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: fire had been weapon, symbol, title, and shame before it was warmth. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He showed me breath, heat, and how to stop before strength became spectacle. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I told him I saw a man choosing what power was for. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the dragons he supposedly defeated. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“Power changes when its reason changes.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through embers, breath, and fire without conquest as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He let himself be proud of life after the sword. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I warmed his hands around a cup of tea.

The kettle whistled before either of us spoke, and Iroh looked proud of the ordinary life around us.

The kettle sang before either of us spoke. Iroh looked proud of the ordinary life we had made around it. We turned out the lamp and listened to the kettle cool. We turned out the lamp and listened to the kettle cool.

bridge_outro: The shop kettle had hardly stopped steaming when a small brass bell rang from Jasmine Steps. Iroh and I crossed into the Lanternweald to find Severus standing beside the community garden, frowning at a plant label. 'This is not mountain mint,' he informed Iroh. 'It has been mislabeled.' I waited for offense. Instead Iroh looked closely at the leaves and asked for a lesson. By sunset, the two had produced a precise growing chart, an excellent pot of tea, and only one argument about whether measurements were a substitute for good judgment. Seeing Iroh learn without pretending to know everything made me love him in another, quieter way.
